# Bit Shifts — Multiply or Divide by Powers of Two

## The identity to remember

$$
n\cdot2^k=n\ll k
$$

**Every symbol explained:** n is a nonnegative integer, k is a nonnegative shift count, and ≪ shifts the binary digits left by k positions in an unbounded-integer model.

**Substitute actual numbers:** For n=5 (binary 101), left shift two places gives binary 10100=20; arithmetic says 5×2²=20.

## Why it is true

Every binary digit's place value doubles when shifted one position left; shifting k positions multiplies all place values by 2^k.

## Algorithm or number puzzle application

Use for constructing bit masks and powers of two, or reasoning about binary-indexed structures.

## Assumptions and pitfalls

To check whether bit i is set, compute n & (1≪i), where & means bitwise AND. For n=5,i=2, 5&4=4 ≠0.

## Your turn

In fixed-width languages high bits may overflow, and right shifts on negative signed values can have different semantics. Do not treat shifts as safe replacements for every arithmetic operation.

**Memory rule:** Remember the mathematical structure behind the bit or counting operation, not a memorised code template.
